To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in Madin-Dary canine kidney cells glycosylation of aquaporin is not essential for the vasopressin dependent insertion of aquaporin into the apical plasma membrane.
the glycosylation of aquaporin 2 is not important for the vasopressin dependent routing of aquaporins in Madin-Dary canine kidney cells.

the vasopressin-stimulated transcellular osmolarity-dependent water permeability (PDW) of Madin-Darhy canine kidney cells transfected with human AQP2 cDNA was reduced by 50% after pretreatment with tunicamcin, a glycosylation inhibitor, but the cAMP-stimulated PDW was not affected.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the glycosylated and unglycosylates forms of aquaporin (AQP)-2 and their role in vasopressin (VP)-induced trafficking of AQP-2 in transfetted cells.
the function of AQP2 glycoylation in Madin-Darbey canine kidney cells.
the role of glycosylation in vasopressin-stimulated trafficking of AQP2.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the extent of glycosylated AQP2 is low in human kidney, and the extent of glycoylation of AQP in human kidney is not important for its routing.
glycosylation is not important for the routing of Aqp2, but is important for the stability and function of the Aqp2 protein.
glycosylation does not seem to be essential for the routing of Aqp2 in the kidney.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
glycosylation is not necessary for routing of AQP-2.
AQP2 in kidney and urine is partially glycosylated and that this glycosylation is not necessary for proper routing of AQP-2 in Madin Darby Canine Kidney cells.
AQP2 in collecting duct is glycosylatied to a varying degree in different individuals, but that glycosylation does not affect its routing.

the vasopressin-activated transcellular osmolarity pathway is not dependent on glycosylation of aquaporin2 in Madin Darby Canine Kidney cells.
the presence of a single glycosylation site on the protein is not sufficient to ensure glycosylation.
